newsitem.title: UK: New green rates shift goalposts for EU farmers.
newsitem.headline: New green rates shift goalposts for EU farmers.

text.p: A round of changes to European Union "green rates" will mean changes in five of its member states to the real value of the prices, subsidies and levies set under EU farm policy.

Green rates are notional currency rates of exchange used by the EU to convert such things as farm subsidies that are set in ecus. The system was designed to insulate farmers from the vagaries of foreign exchange markets.

But, although supposed to create stability, in its present form with changes to rates every 10 days and a grotesquely complicated formula based on actual exchange rates for calculating these, it does not always succeed.
But the four nations that are seeing a devaluation in their green rates - Austria, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands - will not be complaining.

Devaluation raises the values in a country's national currency of all the subsidies paid to its farmers as well as of the prices of goods eligible for support through the EU's intervention buying-in system.
The biggest beneficiaries from a devaluation in recent times have been British farmers, still basking in extra profits they are making following a slide in sterling earlier in the 1990s.

Complaints will be coming from Ireland, which sees its green rate revalued from Saturday under changes announced on Friday. The agrimonetary system is carefully slewed so as to make revaluations next to impossible, because the EU feels that farmers, unlike almost everyone else, should be protected against the adverse effects of having a strong currency.
But occasionally a a national currency appreciates so fast as to mean that revaluation cannot be avoided under the rules.
It is Ireland this time because of the relative strenth of its punt, and a rebounding sterling could mean a British revaluation on January 21.
From this Saturday the new rate for the Irish punt will be 0.778173 per Ecu compared with a current 0.812908 per Ecu.

The devaluations are for the Belgian franc, which changes to 40.1295 francs from the current 40.0486 francs, the German mark, with a new rate of 1.94738 compared with the current 1.94386, the Dutch guilder, with a new rate of 2.18573 compared with the current 2.18167 and the Austrian schilling, with a new rate of 13.7020, compared with the current 13.6782.
